node-1.label: 17-year-old male presents with 3 days of mouth pain and nonpainful penile erosions

node-2.label: One week prior, he experienced transient anosmia and ageusia that spontaneously resolved; he denied fever, cough, dyspnea, rhinorrhea, and gastrointestinal symptoms

node-3.label: He had taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen before presenting to the emergency department, but no medications before the onset of his mucocutaneous eruption

node-4.label: Physical examination showed he was afebrile with normal vital signs (respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97%); findings included shallow erosions of the vermilion lips and hard palate, circumferential erythematous erosions of the periurethral glans penis, and 5 small vesicles on the trunk and upper extremities, with the remainder of the examination unremarkable

why.why: Pathologist analysis explicitly supports a viral mucocutaneous eruption as the best explanation, citing repeatedly positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR, negative other respiratory pathogens and Mycoplasma IgM, transient anosmia/ageusia, no pre-eruption medications, and oral/genital erosions with truncal vesicles. Mycoplasma IgG elevation is interpreted as past infection and does not change the acute viral trigger judgment. Skin biopsy/DIF and HSV/VZV/enterovirus serology remain pending, so confidence is raised from 0.85 to 0.9.

The now-confirmed positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR provides a clear viral trigger, and there were no medications before the eruption. Expert analyses emphasize the absence of a precipitating drug and favor a viral cause; although SJS/TEN remains incompletely excluded, the virologic evidence further reduces the likelihood of drug eruption, lowering confidence from 0.15 to 0.1.

Confirmed COVID-19 and negative Mycoplasma IgM support a viral cause, and there is no autoimmune history. Skin biopsy/DIF is still pending, so autoimmune bullous disease cannot be fully excluded, but the new virologic evidence makes it less likely; confidence is lowered from 0.1 to 0.08.

Confirmed COVID-19 infection, widespread vesicular/oral involvement, and a viral prodrome are atypical for an STI. The new virologic evidence and expert consensus favoring a viral mucocutaneous eruption make an STI unlikely; confidence is lowered from 0.05 to 0.03.

node-9.label: COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) infection with associated mucocutaneous eruption

why.why: Pathologist analysis concludes that COVID-19-related erythema multiforme is the most likely diagnosis, reinforcing the association between confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and the mucocutaneous eruption. Repeatedly positive PCR, negative other respiratory pathogens/Mycoplasma IgM, anosmia/ageusia, and absence of precipitating medication all support this. Mycoplasma IgG is a past-infection marker, not an acute trigger. Pending biopsy/serology leave minor uncertainty; confidence raised from 0.8 to 0.85.

node-10.label: Erythema multiforme associated with viral infection

why.why: Pathologist analysis specifically identifies COVID-19-related erythema multiforme as most likely, and the clinical pattern of oral and genital erosions plus truncal vesicles is characteristic of infection-associated erythema multiforme. Mycoplasma IgG elevation is past infection and does not alter the viral trigger. Skin biopsy/DIF and HSV/VZV/enterovirus serology are still pending, so confidence is raised from 0.4 to 0.5.

node-11.label: SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal PCR was repeatedly positive

node-12.label: Testing for other respiratory pathogens and Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM was negative

node-13.label: Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgG was elevated, indicating past infection rather than acute trigger

node-14.label: Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence has not yet been reported

node-15.label: HSV/VZV/enterovirus serology results are not yet available

why.why: Pathologist analysis explicitly states that current data support COVID-19-related erythema multiforme as the most likely diagnosis, based on repeatedly positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR, negative other respiratory pathogens and Mycoplasma IgM, transient anosmia/ageusia, no pre-eruption medications, and mucocutaneous erosions/vesicles. Mycoplasma IgG elevation is past infection and does not change the acute viral trigger judgment. Pending skin biopsy/DIF and HSV/VZV/enterovirus serology prevent full exclusion of autoimmune bullous disease, HSV/Mycoplasma-related EM, and drug eruption; confidence raised from 0.35 to 0.55.

Pathologist analysis identifies COVID-19-associated erythema multiforme as the most likely diagnosis, supported by confirmed active COVID-19, negative other respiratory pathogens/Mycoplasma IgM, anosmia/ageusia, no precipitating medication, and the characteristic mucocutaneous pattern. Mycoplasma IgG elevation represents past infection rather than an acute trigger. Skin biopsy/DIF and HSV/VZV/enterovirus serology are pending, so autoimmune bullous disease, HSV/Mycoplasma-related EM, and drug eruption are not fully excluded; confidence raised from 0.45 to 0.6.

Pathologist analysis favors erythema multiforme over a nonspecific COVID-19 exanthem because of the characteristic oral and genital mucosal erosions with truncal vesicles. Although confirmed COVID-19 supports a viral exanthem, the clinical morphology and expert opinion make the non-erythema-multiforme exanthem less likely; confidence reduced from 0.25 to 0.15.

attrs.why: Refines the viral mucocutaneous eruption frontier by considering herpes simplex virus as a specific pathogen. The presence of oral and genital erosions (node-4) is classic for HSV, and HSV serology is still pending (node-15), so HSV cannot be excluded. However, confirmed COVID-19 and widespread truncal vesicles make HSV less likely than a COVID-19-driven process.

Refines the frontier by considering varicella-zoster virus as a specific cause. Truncal and extremity vesicles (node-4) could be consistent with VZV, and VZV serology is pending (node-15). However, the prominent oral/genital mucosal erosions and confirmed active COVID-19 reduce the likelihood of VZV as the primary trigger.

Refines the frontier by considering enterovirus as a possible viral trigger, since enterovirus serology is pending (node-15) and can cause oral/genital ulcers with vesicles. Nevertheless, repeatedly positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR and negative testing for other respiratory pathogens make enterovirus a much less likely cause than COVID-19.

node-1.label: 17-year-old male presents with 3 days of mouth pain and nonpainful penile erosions

node-2.label: One week prior, he experienced transient anosmia and ageusia that spontaneously resolved; he denied fever, cough, dyspnea, rhinorrhea, and gastrointestinal symptoms

node-3.label: He had taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen before presenting to the emergency department, but no medications before the onset of his mucocutaneous eruption

node-4.label: Physical examination showed he was afebrile with normal vital signs (respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97%); findings included shallow erosions of the vermilion lips and hard palate, circumferential erythematous erosions of the periurethral glans penis, and 5 small vesicles on the trunk and upper extremities, with the remainder of the examination unremarkable

why.why: Pathologist analysis explicitly supports a viral mucocutaneous eruption as the best explanation, citing repeatedly positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR, negative other respiratory pathogens and Mycoplasma IgM, transient anosmia/ageusia, no pre-eruption medications, and oral/genital erosions with truncal vesicles. Mycoplasma IgG elevation is interpreted as past infection and does not change the acute viral trigger judgment. Skin biopsy/DIF and HSV/VZV/enterovirus serology remain pending, so confidence is raised from 0.85 to 0.9.

Confirmed COVID-19 infection, widespread vesicular/oral involvement, and a viral prodrome are atypical for an STI. The new virologic evidence and expert consensus favoring a viral mucocutaneous eruption make an STI unlikely; confidence is lowered from 0.05 to 0.03.
